subject: 💪 Strong jobs
body_html:
Plus: Fed contradictions | Friday, November 06, 2026
 
View in browser
 
 
Axios Macro
By Neil Irwin and Courtenay Brown · Nov 06, 2026

🔥Wow. The October jobs report offered the strongest all-around set of numbers about the state of the U.S. labor market we've seen in quite a while.

  • We unpack it below, then look at the implications for Federal Reserve policy — particularly against the backdrop of Thursday's steep market sell-off that points to financial conditions tightening.

📊 Situational awareness: University of Michigan consumer sentiment rose 3 points in early November, according to its preliminary survey that ended the day before the midterm elections.

  • Consumers expressed growing anxiety about a possible AI bubble, though those worries were dwarfed by frustration over high prices.

Today's newsletter, edited by George Moriarty and copy edited by Katie Lewis, is 1,003 words, a 4-minute read.
 
 
1 big thing: Big hiring surprise
 
Data: Bureau of Labor Statistics; Chart: Courtenay Brown/Axios

The American job market looks remarkably strong.

  • Employers are hiring at a faster pace than almost any economist anticipated, unemployment remains historically low and wages continue to rise.

Why it matters: There are plenty of reasons businesses might be reluctant to hire, including geopolitical uncertainty and the proliferation of AI. Yet the blockbuster report shows employers have continued to add workers at a robust pace, and layoffs remain low across the economy.

What they're saying: "While much of this year's payroll figures have felt like a 'low hire, low fire,' labor market, October looked more like a 'strong hire, low fire,'" Glenmede's Jason Pride wrote in a note.

By the numbers: Employment rose by 165,000 jobs last month — more than double the 65,000 that economists expected.

  • The previous months' revisions also showed stronger hiring heading into the fall months than previously believed. Payroll gains for August and September were revised upward by a combined 84,000 jobs.
  • The pickup in hiring is particularly striking given how sharply job growth slowed over the summer. Employers have added an average of 137,000 jobs per month over the past three months, compared with a three-month average of just 28,000 from May through July.

Zoom in: Some of the strongest hiring gains came from industries that have struggled to add workers in recent years.

  • Professional and business services — a catch-all category that includes office and administrative jobs — led the gains with 70,000 new positions, far above its average monthly gain of 15,000 over the past year.
  • The manufacturing sector added 19,000 jobs last month, with gains in computer and electronic products, machinery and primary metals.
  • Health care, which has powered much of the nation's job growth in recent years, added another 42,000 workers last month.

Zoom out: The unemployment rate was down to 4.1%, from 4.2% in September (though thanks to rounding, the actual change was smaller than it appears: only 0.03 percentage point), extending a remarkable stretch of stability in the labor market.

  • Even as hiring fluctuated this year, the unemployment rate has barely budged — remaining in a tight range of 4.1% to 4.3% since March.
  • The economy absorbed an influx of workers without pushing unemployment higher: the labor force grew by 421,000, while the number of employed Americans rose by an even bigger 463,000 last month.

One sign of strain: Those working part-time — either because they couldn't find full-time jobs or had their hours cut — surged by 339,000 to 4.8 million last month.

What to watch: Average hourly earnings rose 0.4%, the strongest monthly gain since the start of 2026.

  • Still, annual wage growth has cooled considerably, to 3.1% from 3.9% a year earlier.
  • Inflation has eaten into those gains in recent months. (Tuesday's October Consumer Price Index report will show whether purchasing power improved last month.)

The bottom line: Democrats' sweeping midterm victories underscored Americans' frustration with the high cost of living. But for all that frustration, the job market offers some reason for optimism.

2. Conflicting signals for the Fed
 

Federal Reserve chairman Kevin Warsh speaks at a press conference in Washington, D.C. last week. Photo: Al Drago/Getty Images
 

Looked at in isolation, the new jobs numbers bolster the case for more interest rate increases from the Fed. Monetary policy decisions, however, don't happen in isolation.

The big picture: The strong October labor market data comes at a moment when inflation, not employment, is the Fed's predominant focus. And it comes after the worst day for financial markets in 18 months, which raised the risk that a broader tightening of financial conditions is underway.

  • The new data probably doesn't lock in the kinds of further interest rate hikes that it might against a different backdrop — or a different policy conjuncture, to use chairman Kevin Warsh's favorite phrase.

State of play: Some of the aspects the Fed most scrutinizes for evidence of labor market tightening are showing clear signs of heat, particularly the surge in average hourly earnings and downtick in the unemployment rate.

  • Fed officials have signaled the second interest rate increase this year is likely at a meeting next month, but it is less clear whether further tightening is on the way in 2027.
  • They have indicated that elevated inflation is their foremost concern right now, amid broad stability in the job market outlook.

The intrigue: Yesterday's market sell-off raised the prospect that the froth may be coming out of the AI/data center boom that has powered overall economic growth forward — and contributed to higher inflation — this year.

  • If that continues in the weeks ahead, it raises the prospect that the Fed will be done hiking rates after December, as officials see the market doing the work of tightening for them.

Of note: Moves in bond and futures markets support the idea that, while the jobs numbers point toward more rate increases, the report wasn't a game-changer for monetary policy.

  • The two-year Treasury yield, most sensitive to policy, was up a mere 0.04 percentage point earlier this morning.

What they're saying: "The latest jobs data suggest labor market conditions are tightening, and with inflation well above target, that adds to the case for a December rate hike," wrote Matthew Martin, senior U.S. economist at Oxford Economics, in a note.

  • "However, given most of the core inflation overshoot we expect is tied to spillovers from higher energy prices and AI-related pressures, continued falls in tech stocks and oil prices could eliminate the prospect of an additional hike in early 2027," he added.
